Advance access publication 20 July 2023 Brief Report Etiology, morphology, and outcomes of adrenal calcifications in 540 adult patients—a retrospective singlecenter study Annop Kittithaworn, † Prerna Dogra, † Division of Endocrinology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN 55905, USA *Corresponding author: Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes, Metabolism and Nutrition, Mayo Clinic, 200 First Street SW, Rochester, MN 55905, USA.
Email: Bancos.Irina@mayo.edu Leili Rahimi, Rashi Sandooja, and Irina Bancos*
Abstract Sparse data are available on the etiology, morphology, clinical presentation, and outcomes of adrenal calcification.

In this singlecenter retrospective study of 540 consecutive patients (median age 65 years, 45% women) with adrenal calcification on computed tomography (December 2017 to January 2021), most were discovered incidentally (472, 87%).
The commonest etiology was idiopathic (389, 72%), followed by the adrenal tumor (113, 21%), hemorrhage (29, 5%), and infiltrative disease (7, 1%).
Calcified adrenal tumors were predominantly benign (92, 81%) and primarily adenomas (63, 69%), whereas the most common calcified adrenal malignancy (16, 18%) was metastasis (12, 67%).
Calcification (unilateral 94%, bilateral 6%) morphology varied from punctate (313, 58%) to coarse (165, 30%), linear/curvilinear (46, 9%), and rimlike (16, 3%).
In summary, adrenal calcifications are usually incidentally discovered unilateral, punctate, or coarse lesions of unclear etiology.
Most calcified adrenal tumors are benign and <20% malignant or pheochromocytomas.
Keywords: computed tomography, calcified, adrenal tumor, primary adrenal insufficiency, adrenal mass Significance Existing literature on adrenal calcification is mainly limited to case reports.
We evaluated a large cohort of adult patients with adrenal calcification and found that most were idiopathic.
A fifth of all adrenal calcifications were associated with an underlying adrenal tumor.
Most calcified adrenal tumors were benign and predominantly adenomas, whereas metastasis represented the most common malignant etiology.
No specific calcification morphology was pathognomonic of a malignant adrenal tumor.
The findings of this study, for the first time in the literature, provide an insight into the clinical presentation, various etiological associations, and morphology of adrenal calcifications.
Introduction

The deposition of calcium in blood vessels, organs, and tumors may reflect an underlying pathology, disease severity, or chronicity.1–3 Adrenal calcification may be a result of a previous adrenal hemorrhage, infection, and inflammation or occur within an adrenal tumor.4–9 Our understanding of adrenal calcification remains poor, with published literature limited to case reports on primarily infants and children, several review articles, and 2 small case series of patients with calcified adrenal masses, including 1 that was published more than 3 decades ago.5–9

Keeping in mind the knowledge gaps, the paucity of current literature, and the increased radiological incidence of adrenal calcification, we designed our current study to determine the etiological associations and describe the clinical presentation, morphology, and outcomes of adrenal calcification.

Methods Study design and patient selection This is a retrospective cohort study that was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Mayo Clinic and complies with the Declaration of Helsinki.
A research consent waiver was used.
We employed 2 search strategies to identify adult patients with adrenal calcification between January 1, 2017, and December 31, 2021.

First, we electronically interrogated our institutional radiology database for patients who underwent computed tomography (CT) imaging of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and thoracic or lumbar spine over the 5 year study period using the search terms “adrenal” combined with “calcification” or “calcified.”
This search revealed 471 (0.14%) patients out of the 342 298 unique patients with CT imaging performed.

The electronic search of the Adrenal Mass Database resulted in 571 potential patients with a calcified adrenal tumor (after excluding 248 patients that overlapped with the radiology database) during the study period.
The search results of the 2 databases were combined, and radiology reports and associated CT images were reviewed.
Those with unavailable CT images or lack of calcification associated with adrenal gland(s) or tumors were excluded.

Data collection Medical records of patients in the final cohort were reviewed, and information was gathered on demographics, mode of initial discovery, etiology, imaging characteristics, and outcomes.

Computed tomography images were analyzed for the adrenal calcification laterality, number, morphology (punctate, coarse, linear/curvilinear, and rimlike/eggshell), and association with an adrenal mass and location (peripheral, septal, central, and combination)
(Figure 1).

As described in the literature, calcification was identified as bright white spots and unenhanced attenuation of ≥100 Hounsfield units on CT imaging.3 Outcomes of interest were etiology and if associated with an adrenal mass—malignancy.
Malignancy was diagnosed based on histopathology.
For calcifications without evidence of an apparent underlying cause, etiology was labeled as “idiopathic.”

Subgroup comparisons were made based on the calcification laterality (unilateral vs bilateral), association with an underlying adrenal tumor (with vs without adrenal tumors), and nature of the adrenal tumor (benign vs malignant).
Statistical analysis We presented categorical data as counts and percentages and continuous data as median and interquartile ranges (IQR).
The association between variables was assessed using the chi- square test and Wilcoxon/Kruskal–Wallis test.
Statistical significance was defined as a Pvalue of <.05.

Statistical analyses were conducted using the JMP Software, version 16.1.0, SAS Institute Inc. Results Over the 5 year study duration, radiological evidence of adrenal calcification was noted in 540 patients at a median age of 65 years (IQR, 5474), comprising 245 (45%) women and 512 (95%) White individuals.
Adrenal calcification was discovered incidentally on CT imaging performed for unrelated reasons in 472 (87%) patients, during cancer staging imaging in 66 (12%), and for other reasons in 2 (1%).
Only 167 (31%) patients were evaluated by an endocrinologist.

The etiology of adrenal calcification was idiopathic in 389 (72%), related to an underlying adrenal tumor in 113 (21%), adrenal hemorrhage in 29 (5%), and infiltrative disease (infectious or inflammatory) in 7 (1%) patients.
Of the 113 patients with adrenal tumors, benign tumors were diagnosed in 92 (81%), adrenal malignancy in 18 (16%), and pheochromocytomas in 2 (2%), and 1 (1%) patient had an inflammatory pseudotumor.
Among the 92 benign adrenal tumors, most were adrenal adenomas (63, 69%), and for the 18 malignant tumors, metastases (12, 67%) were the most common.

Overall, only 7 (1%) patients had associated primary adrenal insufficiency, diagnosed before the appearance of calcification in all, and 18 (3%) underwent adrenalectomy, primarily due to concern for underlying malignancy (Table 1).
Adrenal calcification(s) were unilateral in 506 (94%) patients (right 264, 49%; left 242, 45%) and bilateral in 34 (6%), with the majority presenting as a single calcification (415, 77%).
The most common calcification morphology was punctate (313, 58%), followed by coarse (165, 30%), linear or curvilinear (46, 9%), and rimlike (16, 3%).
When associated with an adrenal tumor, the pattern of calcification was central in 51 (45%), peripheral in 43 (38%), septal in 10 (9%), and multiple locations in 9 (8%) patients (Figure 2, Table 1).

Compared to patients with unilateral adrenal calcification, those with bilateral involvement were more likely to be discovered during cancer staging (18% vs 12%, P = .02), have associated primary adrenal insufficiency (12% vs 1%, P < .0001), present as multiple (53% vs 21%, P < .0001) and coarse lesions (62% vs 28%, P < .0001), and to be associated with an adrenal tumor in multiple locations (40% vs 5%, P = .001)
(Table 1).
Patients with calcified adrenal tumors, compared to those with nonneoplastic calcification, were slightly younger with a higher proportion of women (Table 2).

Subgroup analysis of malignant vs benign tumors revealed no difference in the calcification morphology, but those with malignant tumors were less likely to present with calcifications in peripheral (11% vs 43%) or septal (5% vs 10%) locations (P = .03) (Table 2).

Outcomes in a consecutive cohort of adult patients.

We found that almost all adrenal calcifications were discovered on imaging performed for evaluation of a nonadrenal pathology and usually presented as single, unilateral, punctate, or coarse lesions of unclear etiology.
We also found that most adrenal tumors demonstrating calcification were benign; however, adrenal malignancy and pheochromocytomas represented 18% of patients with adrenal tumors.
Most patients in our cohort were between 50 and 70 years, likely explained by a higher prevalence of comorbidities prompting the need for radiological investigations with advancing age.
Despite the increased use of radiological examinations, we found adrenal calcifications to be rare, reported on 0.14% of abdominal CT scans.

The 2 prior studies focused only on patients with calcified adrenal tumors, 1 being a surgical series and another published more than 3 decades ago describing mainly nonincidental cases, thereby limiting the evaluation of other etiological associations.7,9
In contrast, in our study, we used broader inclusion criteria and identified patients from 2 separate institutional databases.

Though we found that most adrenal calcifications were idiopathic, approximately 30% had an identifiable etiology, with an underlying adrenal tumor being the most common, followed by hemorrhage and, rarely, a benign infiltrative disease.
Notably, most calcified adrenal tumors were benign and predominantly adenomas but also included myelolipomas and adrenal cysts.
For the minority with underlying adrenal malignancy, most were adrenal metastases, and less than onefourth represented either adrenocortical cancer or pheochromocytoma.

In a recent study by Yalon et al.,16 where they defined and evaluated a novel 9variable imagebased score to differentiate adrenocortical carcinomas and lipidpoor adrenal adenomas, calcification was negatively predictive of adrenocortical carcinoma.
Despite the differences in the study design and cohort selection, these findings align with our observations that most calcified adrenal tumors are benign.
In our study, we reviewed imaging characteristics in all patients and appreciated various morphologies of adrenal calcifications.

While we found no specific calcification morphology that distinguished malignant from benign adrenal tumors with 100% accuracy, we noted that the peripheral or septal location of calcification was less likely to be associated with malignant tumors.

In addition to the large sample size, the strengths of our study are the inclusion of consecutive patients irrespective of etiology or management, thereby enabling a better understanding of the prevalence, etiological associations, and outcomes in adrenal calcifications.
Nonetheless, our study has certain limitations mainly related to the retrospective singlecenter design that led to information and selection bias and the short duration of our study.

Our study’s adult and predominantly White population from the northern midwest region of the United States may have had an impact on the prevalence of certain etiologies and limit the generalizability of these findings to children, nonWhite races, and those in different geographical locations.
As the diagnosis of calcification was based on the availability of CT, imaging bias is present in our assessment of the calcification prevalence.
We also acknowledge the lack of histopathology in most of our cohort, including those with adrenal tumors; however, given the unique presentation on CT, misdiagnosis of calcification was unlikely.

The rare occurrence of primary adrenal insufficiency in our study could be an underestimation, especially in patients with bilateral adrenal metastasis, as many were likely not evaluated for adrenal insufficiency.15 In conclusion, adrenal calcifications are incidentally discovered lesions with a radiological prevalence of 0.14%, typically presenting as unilateral, punctate, or coarse lesions of unclear etiology.
Only a fifth of calcifications is associated with an underlying adrenal tumor.
Most adrenal tumors with associated calcifications are benign, with less than 20% representing a pheochromocytoma or an adrenal malignancy.
No specific calcification morphology helps distinguish malignant from benign adrenal tumors with 100% accuracy.
